titulo.en: Sound of the day: b and v

texto.en: In Spanish, the letters b and v stand for exactly the same sound. Their names are different (be and uve), but the sound is identical. At the beginning of a word or after m or n it is like the b in “boy”: bien, vivo, también. After a vowel it is softer: the lips barely touch, and the teeth never touch the lip (trabajo, hablo). Never say a Spanish v like the English v. Say them slowly: bien, vivo, trabajo, hablo, también.

Verbs in the dictionary form (the infinitive) end in -ar, -er or -ir. Today: -ar verbs, like hablar (to speak), trabajar (to work) and estudiar (to study). Remove -ar and add an ending that shows who is acting: yo -o (hablo), tú -as (hablas), usted / él / ella -a (habla), nosotros -amos (hablamos), ustedes / ellos / ellas -an (hablan). Because the ending already shows the person, Spanish usually drops the pronoun: say Trabajo en el instituto, not Yo trabajo en el instituto. Use the pronoun only to contrast or stress: Yo trabajo y ella estudia. The present covers both English forms: trabajo means “I work” and “I am working”. Use trabajar en + place (trabajo en el instituto). A subject you study takes no article: estudio español, estudio arquitectura. To ask a friend, use tú: ¿Trabajas o estudias? To ask an older person, use usted: ¿Trabaja o estudia? Emma uses tú with Daniela.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: c, z and s

texto.en: In Latin America, the letters s, z, and c before e or i all sound like s: la cena, la ciudad, zapato. Before a, o or u, the letter c is a hard k sound: casa, como. Both sounds meet in cocina: the first c is a k, the second is an s (“koh-SEE-nah”). Say them slowly: cena, ciudad, cocina, casa, como.

Verbs in -er (comer, aprender, leer) and -ir (vivir, escribir) use almost the same endings as -ar verbs, but with e where -ar has a: yo -o (como, vivo), tú -es (comes, vives), usted / él / ella -e (come, vive), nosotros -emos or -imos (comemos, vivimos), ustedes / ellos / ellas -en (comen, viven). The only difference between -er and -ir is nosotros: -emos with -er verbs and -imos with -ir verbs. Everything else is the same. As with -ar verbs, drop the pronoun: Vivo en Quito, Aprendo español. Use en + city to say where you live. In Los Andrade, los means “the” before more than one person; you will learn plurals later. Emma uses usted with Señora Rosa and tú with Daniela.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: g and j

texto.en: The letters ge, gi and j sound like a strong h, a bit rougher than the English h: ingeniero, ingeniera, jugo. Before a, o or u, the letter g is a hard g as in “go”: gato. titulo.en: Professions: masculine, feminine, and no article

texto.en: To ask what someone does for a living, use ¿A qué te dedicas? with a friend (tú) and ¿A qué se dedica usted? with an older person or someone you don't know well (usted). Literally it means “what do you dedicate yourself to?”. Answer with ser + the profession, and without an article: Soy profesora, Mateo es diseñador (not “soy una profesora”). Many professions have two forms: -o for a man and -a for a woman (el profesor, la profesora; el ingeniero, la ingeniera), and -or for a man and -ora for a woman (el diseñador, la diseñadora). Some words are the same for both: el estudiante and la estudiante, el taxista and la taxista; only the article changes. A woman says Soy profesora; a man says Soy profesor. Add de + subject to say more: profesora de inglés.
Most professions change their ending; some stay the same. Tap each word to hear it.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: stress and the written accent

texto.en: In Spanish, a word is stressed on one syllable, and the written accent (the tilde) is a mark that shows it. A word stressed on the last syllable gets a tilde if it ends in -n, -s or a vowel: inglés (een-GLÉS), francés, alemán, portugués. A word stressed on the last syllable that ends in a different consonant gets no tilde: español (es-pah-NYOL), universidad. Without the tilde, the word would be read with a different stress, so always write it: inglés, not “ingles”. Say them slowly: inglés, francés, alemán, portugués, español.

titulo.en: Languages and how well you speak them

texto.en: To talk about languages, use hablar with no article: Hablo inglés, not “hablo el inglés”. Names of languages are not capitalized: inglés, español, francés. To say how well, put the level after the language: muy bien (very well), más o menos (so-so), and un poco de + language for “a little”: Hablo un poco de español. To say you don't speak one, put no before the verb: No hablo francés. To ask a friend or someone your age, use tú: ¿Qué idiomas hablas? To ask an older person or someone you don't know well, use usted: ¿Qué idiomas habla usted? Idioma means “language”; idiomas means “languages”. Answer with hablo: Hablo inglés y un poco de español.

nota.en: Literally “it is pleasing to me”.

explicacion.en: In English “I” is the subject; in Spanish the thing you like is the subject, so the verb is gusta.
Don't use yo gusto. Use me gusta + the thing you like.
After gusta, use the infinitive (bailar), not a conjugated form.

texto.en: The letters ch sound like the ch in “cheese”: chocolate, mucho, escuchar, noche, chao. In Spanish, ch is a single sound, and it is always like this, never like a k or like sh. Say them slowly: chocolate, mucho, escuchar, noche, chao.

In English you are the one who likes something: “I like coffee”. In Spanish, the thing you like is the subject, so it works more like “coffee is pleasing to me”. That is why gusta stays the same (with one thing or an infinitive), and only me, te or le changes: me gusta (I like), te gusta (you like, tú), le gusta (he / she likes, or you like, usted). After gusta, use el or la with a singular noun (me gusta el café, me gusta la música) or an infinitive (me gusta bailar). To say you don't like something, put no before the whole phrase: no me gusta el fútbol. To name the person, add a + name: a Daniela le gusta bailar. For contrast, use a mí or a ti. To ask a question, keep the same words and raise your voice at the end: ¿Te gusta el chocolate? Mucho goes after gusta: me gusta mucho el chocolate.
Me, te or le shows who likes it. Tap each phrase to hear it.

consigna.en: Complete: “I don't like coffee.”

feedback.en: No goes before me gusta: no me gusta.

consigna.en: Listen. Does the speaker like music?

feedback.en: No me gusta la música: the speaker does not like music.

consigna.en: Write in Spanish: “I like chocolate.”

feedback.en: Me gusta el chocolate. Use el before the noun.

aceptadas: A mí me gusta el chocolate.

consigna.en: Write in Spanish: “Do you like coffee?” (tú)

feedback.en: ¿Te gusta el café? Te for tú.
